frontText:
Many projects require specific knowledge to 
understand the context or problem. Asking experts 
is often the most direct and efficient way to get the 
needed information.
Experts can not only answer precisely what you 
need to know but might be able to direct you to 
other topics or people to talk to that you might not 
have considered before.
backText:
Get a sound recorder and a notebook to record your insights.
Brainstorm as a team on topics you would like to discuss with the 
participant; the more, the better. Finally, discuss the issues and agree 
on 3-5 good topics.
Formulate questions for each topic - ensure you only have a few 
questions and avoid yes or no questions.
Having at least two people during the interview is best. But agree on 
your roles - who interviews and who takes notes? 
Contact the expert. If you need help figuring out where to start, 
begin by contacting the person in your network who best fits the 
profile you need. Tell them about your project and ask them whether 
they could answer it for you or if they can recommend someone they 
know who would be more suitable. Follow this chain of people for as 
many steps as you find relevant.
a. Formulate your questions and ask the participant to provide concrete 
examples and stories. Make sure you do not assume anything, ask 
“why” and “how“ several times for more detailed explanations.
b. Take this chance to ask for advice on specific challenges and to get 
directed to the right people to explore the topic further.
c. Record the interview to capture accurate quotes of the 
participant’s words and use your notes to capture essential points.

frontText:
Share to have a shared view! 
Story share & capture is an alignment tool typically 
used after ethnographic research.
With this method, each team member shares 
their gathered insights with the team. It brings 
everyone on the same page when team members 
use different research methods. It sparks and 
facilitates discussions that deeper explore the 
research themes.
backText:
Share the research findings with the team members by letting 
everyone know beforehand and asking them to organise and bring 
their insights to the session.
The team takes turns sharing their learnings from the field research 
they have performed through stories and notes.
Others write down what they find the most important in the form 
of insights, headings or quotes on individual Post-its. Everyone 
places post-its on a wall in relation to one another to create a 
shared overview.
Review all insights together at the end of the session. Re-organise and 
cluster insights iteratively until everyone agrees with the final overview.

frontText:
Put a number on it! 
Surveys can fit your problem and can be an 
excellent way to support or see the prevalence of 
your insights in a quantitative way.
Statistics can help decision-making and validate 
choices.
backText:
Decide why you need the survey and what insights are best gathered 
through quantitative methods vs. qualitative ones.
Choose a sample size that would be meaningful to get feedback from 
for your project.
Write a set of questions to which you want aggregated answers. To 
create and distribute online surveys, use tools such as Google Forms. 
Otherwise, a paper survey can sometimes be better to target the 
right audience.
Test your survey to ensure everything is understandable and clear to 
the reader. Iterate through it until you are satisfied.
Distribute the survey and collect the answers.
Aggregate the data if it isn’t automatically done for you. Analyse the 
results, e.g. look for any unexpected outcomes or if it validates any of 
your qualitative findings.

frontText:
Take a close look at a situation! 
Observations provide deep insights into 
opportunities and challenges that only emerge in 
some particular situations.
By using observations, we see the difference 
between what people say and what they do.
We often use observations to see how people use 
products and services in different situations or 
manage without them.
backText:
Find a sound recorder and a notebook to record your insights.
Brainstorm from your knowledge about the challenge, who/what you 
want to observe, and in what situations. The more suggestions, the 
better. Discuss them and agree on how you want to proceed.
Write an observation guide describing your approach in detail. What 
products, services and use situations do you particularly want to 
observe? How will you observe (notes, video and pictures)? Format 
for your data/notes, e.g. ”What do people do, how do they do it, and 
why do they do it”.
Get the necessary permissions, e.g. to film and take pictures - and 
then go!
Tell the participants what the observation is about without priming 
them – i.e. tell them enough to make them feel safe without 
revealing too many details about what you want to get out of the 
observation or your thoughts about what you think they do.
Monitor the situation and influence what is happening as little 
as possible. Capture everything along the way - including your 
impressions and interpretations (for example, in ” Why do they do 
this”).
Interview the participant you have observed afterwards based on 
what you have seen, if relevant and possible.

frontText:
Map it out! 
An actor-network map is a way to visualise the 
actors and the connecting processes around a 
specific cause.
This method is a way to gather findings in an 
organised manner. It guides your team around the 
topic by displaying which causal relationships have 
yet to be explored.
backText:
Map one key actor (human or not) at the centre of your research 
topic. Draw a box around it.
Identify the actors around the central one. These can be human and 
non-human and be intentionally or unintentionally connected to the 
main actor. Draw individual boxes around them.
Assign proximate and root causes to these actors. Proximate causes
are those that immediately result in a specific change. Root causes 
are those which lead to proximate causes. Place proximate-cause 
actors close to the central actor. Place root actors further away.
Draw connections between these actors and label these with 
processes phrased as verbs.
Consider colour coordinating, clustering etc. Remember to add a 
legend for others or yourself in the future.
Based on the first draft, explore areas you need more information 
about to make it more concrete. It can guide your next activity in the 
project. Update Actor-Network Map as you find new information.

frontText:
Talk to people! 
Interviews give us a picture of the different needs 
of our target group as well as inspiration to see 
opportunities we have yet to think of.
Through interviews, we try to see the world from 
the interviewee’s perspective.
We conduct interviews to gather knowledge and 
build empathy to understand users’ behaviour and 
choices in different situations.
backText:
Get a sound recorder and a notebook to record your insights.
Brainstorm as a team topics you would like to discuss with the 
participant; the more, the better. Finally, discuss the issues and agree 
on 3-5 good topics.
Choose an interview form that suits the type of knowledge you 
want, e.g.:
• Intercepts, where you interview the participant for a few minutes 
in a situation where you expect to get excellent answers about 
what they are doing and why.
• In-depth interviews, where you typically interview the participant for 
20 min or longer in a place where you are sure the conversation will 
not be disturbed.
Formulate questions for each topic. Ensure you only have a few 
questions and avoid yes or no questions. Ensure the quantity and 
type of questions match the interview form.
Having at least two people during the interview is best. But agree on 
your roles - who interviews and who takes notes?
• Make the participants feel comfortable and create an informal 
atmosphere.
• Formulate your questions and ask the participant to provide concrete 
examples and stories. Ask “why” several times for more detailed 
explanations, and let the participant tell unexpected stories about 
your topics.
• Record the interview to capture accurate quotes of the 
participant’s words and use your notes to capture essential 
pointers, body language, environment, etc.

frontText:
Keep it rolling! 
For partner-hunting, we use the approach “roll the 
snowball”.
We roll the snowball by finding an expert who 
refers us to another expert, etc. We repeat until 
we have found the appropriate partner.
In this hunting process, we gradually define what 
competencies and personalities we seek and 
collect this ongoingly in a partner profile.
backText:
Print a good stack of profile cards.
Elaborate your design vision or problem so you can quickly explain it 
to a potential partner.
Describe in profile cards who are your desired partners. Fill out as 
many areas as you can. You will describe the remaining ones later. 
Find one person from the area - it does not have to be someone you 
expect to work with, just someone who knows the area better than 
you do.
Call the person, explain your vision and ask what competencies they 
think you need. Ask for the name of someone you can contact further.
Update the profile card with your new insights - and then keep calling, 
explaining the vision, receiving feedback and getting new names.
Continue until you find a partner you are passionate about working with!

frontText:
Take the democratic approach! 
Decision voting can be helpful to converge and 
reduce the number of insights or ideas the team 
will work with.
There are many ways to vote, and you should 
decide which best fits the needs of the task and 
the team. The criteria on which the voting is based 
can also alter the results.
You can choose democratically or use the scoring 
your team gives each element as one of the 
criteria to base the final decision
backText:
Consider what type of voting best fits the team and task: Is it a 
problem if people are influenced by one another? If so, consider 
blind voting, such as voting in an online or physical survey and 
simultaneously lifting a card with a score. If not, you can use dotvoting (placing dot stickers signifying one vote).
Consider if you prefer having the ideas ranked relative to each other 
or scoring them individually from a numerical scale.
Consider whether you will use the votes as one of many criteria to 
inform your choice or directly and democratically follow the outcome 
of the voting exercise to reduce your scope.
Decide on the criteria you will use for the voting; here are some 
suggestions: preference, feasibility or potential user desirability. 
Remember that you can do multiple rounds of voting by using 
different criteria.
Organise the insights or ideas you are voting on, so they are easily 
recognisable, e.g. hanging them on the wall so people can walk 
around and read them.
Ask everyone to take a few minutes to review all of the insights or 
ideas that they will be voting on.
Prompt everyone to vote on the insights or ideas based on your 
chosen criteria and tools. If you use multiple measures, separate 
them into rounds or distinguish them, e.g., through colour-coded 
dot stickers.
Review the outcome with the team and use the votes to start a 
discussion.

frontText:
Feel the mood! 
Empathise and align with other team members 
by creating a moment to share their excitement, 
concerns, feedback and updates.
By checking in and out, you can see the effect of 
the session on participants’ mood and outlook on 
the activity.
This can be done at a specific workshop or as a 
recurring activity in meetings with your team.
backText:
Get your team together in a circle at the beginning of the day (for check-in) 
and at the end of it (for check-out).
Check-in
Define a question which can be general or related to the day’s theme. 
Here are some examples:
• What do I want to learn and focus on today?
• What would I like to contribute to the workshop?
• What are you looking forward to today?
• What inspires me about today?
Take turns around the room to answer so everybody can speak.
Check-out
Similarly, define a common question for the day, e.g.:
• What did you get out of the day?
• What was fun, surprising, and educational?
• What hopes do you have for the next day?
• What feeling are you checking out with?
Take turns around the room to answer so everybody can speak.

frontText:
Discover nuances! 
Participants physically display their opinion and 
viewpoints on chosen topics by placing themselves 
on a scale.
This exercise can break the ice, energise par
backText:
Create a scale by writing each number at each extreme, e.g. 1 and 10 
in a 1-10 scale, on a cardboard card.
Use tape to create a line on the floor to represent the scale from, e.g. 
1 to 10.
Define and pose a question relevant to the day’s theme.
Invite participants to place themselves on the scale and stand in a 
line on the floor.
Ask the participants why they have chosen to stand where they have 
to create a joint discussion between participants.

frontText:
Build people up! 
Providing constructive feedback is a skill that you 
can develop. One way to do this is by following the 
“I like, I wish, what if“ formula.
Feedback is crucial for your team to grow. How- ever, it can also create a hostile atmosphere if 
incorrectly delivered.
backText:
Create a comfortable environment within the team so that feedback is 
received positively. Shape the delivery of the feedback as well as the content 
of it. Here is one example of a model that makes feedback a success, both 
for a deliverer and a recipient of it.
”I Like, I Wish, What If ’’
When delivering feedback:
• Be concrete
• Be constructive and flexible
When receiving feedback:
• Listen actively and have an open mind,
• Say thank you and treat feedback as a gift which you decide if 
you want to act upon.

frontText: Move people! Loosen people up with some physical activities encompassing multiple games and exercises. Stoke will mentally and physically stimulate team members to perform better in the following activities. This activity is e.g. used at the start of the day, right before an exercise that needs people to be very engaged, or when you want to energise the room.
backText:
Find a stoke activity that feels appropriate for your team. A stoke activity 
should require participants to actively engage, listen, think, and do. Here 
are some you can try.
Category, category, die! 
Pick a category.
At a fast pace, point at each person in a random order. When a 
person is pointed at, they must say a word in that category. If they 
can’t, everyone shouts, “ Die!” and they are eliminated for that round.
Sound ball 
Gather in a circle.
Pass an imaginary ball to each other by making eye contact with the 
recipient and making a noise as the ball is thrown.
The recipient must repeat that noise when catching it and make a 
new sound as he throws it to the next person. Add balls around the 
circle or increase the speed to make it more challenging.
“Yes, Let’s” 
Have everyone walk around the room randomly.
One person offers, e.g.” Let’s act like the floor is ice”. Everyone 
responds,” Yes, let’s,” and follows that instruction.
Anyone can make a new offer anytime, and everyone must comply.

frontText: Go in the same direction! ”I do art” is an acronym for a checklist that allows your team to align in a meeting, workshop, or other session. Each” I do art” letter represents Intention, Desired Outcome, Agenda, Roles and rules, and Time.
backText:
Get your team together and go through the following points.

Intention: What is the intent or purpose of the workshop/ meeting? Why are we here?

Desired Outcome / Output: What effect or outcome should result from the workshop? What do we want once the workshop is over?

Agenda: What tasks/exercises/activities should be carried out during the workshop to achieve the desired outcome?

Roles and Rules: What roles are necessary to ensure the workshop’s success? Is there a clear distinction between these roles, e.g. facilitator and participant? Do we need to set some rules at the start?

Time: The time frame for the session, including breaks.

frontText:
Laugh together! 
Draw each other without looking at the paper to 
break the ice and have fun together.
When the workshop’s atmosphere feels heavy 
or formal, this exercise allows users to laugh at 
themselves together.
Use this method to break the ice or as an 
energiser. Getting the participants to bond 
before an exercise in pairs or small groups can be 
especially useful.
backText:
Distribute the necessary drawing materials to each person.
Participants sit in pairs and have only 30 seconds to draw each 
other without looking at the paper. You can play music as the 
participants draw.
Signal the end of the 30 seconds and stop the music. Have everyone 
write the name of the person they drew at the bottom of the paper.
Repeat this for 2 or 3 more rounds with new pairings. 
In the end, everyone will receive 3 or 4 drawings of themselves and 
choose the one that portrays them best.

frontText:
Test hypotheses!
With test cards, we measure the effect we expect 
our concept to have, which until now has only 
been hypothetical.
The test shows whether the concept works in its 
current form and inspires further development 
and marketing.
The test focuses on testing several of the most 
critical hypotheses.
backText:
Print many test cards - you will need one for each of the hypotheses 
you wish to test.
Select a solution to test that has been matured through, e.g. rapid 
feedback matrix. You can also use the method to test minimum viable 
products, i.e. early versions of the final solution that are more than 
just prototypes.
Brainstorm what critical hypotheses (assumptions) you have 
about your solution that will be important to get tested—balance 
hypotheses aimed at users, technology and economic reality.
Complete a test card for each critical hypothesis and determine how 
to measure and test your assumptions. You can research various test 
forms, e.g. focus group tests, usage tests and test actions.
Prioritise your test cards so that the most critical hypotheses, which 
are quick and cheap to test, come first.
Conduct the test as designed on your test card. Often, this involves 
building specialised prototypes and test set-ups such as focus groups 
and long-term tests. 
Find out if your critical hypotheses are valid. If needed, formulate 
additional test cards to learn more about invalid hypotheses and 
underlying factors. Use these test loops to finalise your concept.

frontText:
Get feedback!
Feedback is one of the central parts of design 
thinking. Generally, we want to get feedback as early, 
as quickly, and from as many people as possible.
The Rapid Feedback Matrix requires little 
preparation, enabling you to collect feedback 
quickly. You gather feedback, criticism, questions 
and new ideas systematically.
Often, you combine this method with one or 
more prototyping methods. A prototype offers an 
excellent and concrete basis for feedback gathering.
backText:
Start with a low-fidelity prototype, provotype, or idea you want to 
get feedback on from specific people.
Print the “rapid feedback matrix” template or draw the matrix on a 
whiteboard or flip chart. The matrix can help collect respondents’ 
feedback on prototypes, provotypes and ideas. 
Invite relevant stakeholders to give you feedback. Explain what you 
would like them to provide feedback on. They can be internally in 
your organisation or external experts and users. The model collects 
two types of feedback and two types of reflections:
• A delta symbol represents critical feedback.
• A heart represents positive feedback.
• A question mark represents questions for clarification.
• A light bulb represents new ideas that emerge from the team. 
Stay neutral while collecting and reflecting on the feedback. Try to 
answer all questions with questions.
Discuss learnings in the team right after the test to align 
interpretations and agree on the next steps.

frontText:
Talk as you go!
This method works as it sounds. You encourage the 
test subject – e.g. user or expert - to keep saying 
what they think as they use the solution.
The think-out-loud test is a great way to capture 
where precisely the user struggles using the 
solution, as you will notice even minor frustrations.
Although saying what they think may be daunting 
for users initially, you will get more honest and 
deeper insights once they get used to it.
backText:
Build a medium to high-fidelity prototype of the solution, e.g. 
minimum viable product or early software. All the features you want 
to test need to be included, but nothing else.
Clarify what you want to learn from the test – use, e.g. test cards or 
assumption dump (see cards).
Describe a task, i.e., short instructions explaining what the test 
subjects should try to achieve during the test. Ensure the description 
guides the user away from any non-existing features.
Present the prototype to your users along with the task description 
and let them start the test. Explain that they need to talk constantly 
during the test – to “think out loud”.
Record as much data as possible through video, pictures and 
interview notes during the test. Capture the user’s experience and 
occasionally ask questions, but keep them to a minimum. Don’t help 
them if confused, but capture what they say. 
Finalise the test by analysing your video and audio across multiple 
users. Organise a learning workshop with your team to elicit learnings 
from the data and refine the design.

frontText:
It’s all relative!
This method is typically used during the design 
process to find out how options A and B compare 
against each other, be it two very different 
solutions or two minor features.
A/B testing asks the test subject to choose 
between two particular types of products. It is 
easier for a test subject to evaluate the quality of 
A compared to B than to assess it on its own.
The test subject is only sometimes a user. 
A/B testing can, e.g. be used to ask experts to 
determine which technological direction is best.
backText:
Build two prototypes in the same way. Otherwise, the test subject 
will focus their feedback on the prototyping method rather than 
the concept. Prototypes could be low or high-fidelity. Good options 
are, e.g. prototyping on paper, physical models, or fully functional 
software.
Clarify what you want to learn from the test – use, e.g. test cards or 
assumption dump (see cards). 
Describe a task, i.e., short instructions explaining what the test 
subjects should try to achieve during the test.
Present the two prototypes and the task description to your test 
subject. They perform the task with prototype A and then B. You can 
ask your test subject to “think out loud” during the test (see card).
Ask test subjects to choose their preferred prototype after the test. 
Interview them regarding why and what exactly they liked about each 
prototype. 
Record as much data as possible through video, pictures and 
interview notes.
Use your insights to create a new specification for the next version of 
the design, e.g. “mostly A, but with this feature from B”.

frontText:
How Might We? 
A data-based design question always starts with 
‘How might we...’?
Design questions are the heart of idea 
development. They set the direction for the ideas 
and ensure the connection between user needs 
and our solutions.
Although we must think broadly when creating 
ideas, ideas must always answer the design 
question.
backText:
Write down the issues you have found in your data in an easy-tounderstand format, e.g., jobs-to-be-done.
Print the design question template for everyone.
Everyone formulates at least 3 design questions silently for the 
problem you have chosen to solve. A design question always starts 
with “How might we ...”
Discuss your questions and create more in collaboration – use the 
strategies from the template to strengthen your questions.
Evaluate and adjust the design questions. Make them concrete 
enough to get answers in the form of ideas quickly but sufficiently 
abstract so that there are many possible answers to the same 
question. Think ”why” to lift the level of abstraction and ”how” to 
lower it.
Choose a few of the most inspiring questions for each of your jobs.
Repeat the process until you have formulated design questions for all 
chosen problems.

frontText:
Find jobs that need solving! 
We use jobs-to-be-done to simplify the complex 
data to brief descriptions of jobs our ideas must 
solve for the user.
It is easy to get lost in a large data set, and 
formulating the jobs to be done helps the team 
focus on the most important insights.
Finding all the patterns and jobs in the data set is 
unnecessary - a few deep insights are enough.
backText:
Make your data set easy to understand by putting it on a wall or 
spreading it on a large table.
Find clues in your data set for tasks you can solve. The indications are 
typically in one of the four areas of the structure of a job: [user] who is 
in [situation/context] needs [user’s need] because [cause of need].
Look for needs in the data set based on the 3 main types:
• Functional needs describe specific functions the user tries to do.
• Emotional needs describe how the user wants to feel in a 
particular situation.
• Social needs describe how the user wants to be perceived by others.
Write as many short job descriptions as you can. First, separately, 
without speaking to each other, and then together. Remember, 
the causes of the needs are often not apparent in data but require 
interpreting and comparing different data sources.
Write 3-5 job descriptions in more detail which would be meaningful 
to solve for you and the user.

frontText:
Clear out your brain! 
Dumping your assumptions is an essential step for 
a successful design process, and this method can 
guide you through it.
Acknowledging your assumptions as such enables 
you to take steps to get rid of them and validate or 
invalidate them through research.
This method helps you not only identify 
assumptions but also proposes a mechanism to 
rank them based on how dangerous they are to 
your process and outcome.
backText:
Brainstorm in a group about your assumptions. 
Write out 6 categories of assumptions in the template: customers, 
problem, solution, MVP, competition, and sales channel. Use, ignore 
or adapt categories to fit your problem. Phrase assumptions as 
statements, e.g. for a pizza delivery service, an assumption might be 
“customers have phones available” or “people want to personalise 
their pizzas”.
Iterate until you are happy with the breadth and depth your 
assumptions cover.
Score each assumption 1-5 based on the probability of it being 
wrong. In the above example, it is unlikely that customers will not 
have phones. Thus score is 1.
Score each assumption 1-10 based on the impact of it being wrong. 
In the above example, customers not having phones has a huge 
impact. Thus score is 9.
Multiply the above scores to estimate the risk the assumption would 
have if it were wrong. In the above example, probability 1 x impact 9 
= risk 9
Compare risk scores and identify the most dangerous assumptions 
you hold. Results will help you distribute resources and identify 
necessary research areas.

frontText:
Measure maturity! 
The nine Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) are a 
system to measure the maturity level of a particular 
technology.
The scale goes from the lowest level of maturity 
TRL1 where the basic principles are being observed 
to the highest level of maturity TRL9 where the 
technology has been successfully used in a context 
similar to yours. 
You can use the TRL framework to assess the 
maturity of technology you may want to develop 
or implement into your processes, products and 
services for risk management and decision-making.
backText:
Find the template describing what each TRL means. Ensure everyone 
has the template at hand so they can follow the process.
Identify the specific technology you are considering implementing. 
Research about the technology and its development.
Move upward through the levels in the template, asking if the 
selected technology fulfils them.
Stop at the last fulfilled stage (i.e. fulfilling TRL4 does not move you 
up to TRL5).
Consider if the identified maturity level still fits your needs. 
Evaluate your time, financial resources and the benefits of using this 
technology

frontText:
Follow the user!
A user journey maps the course a user goes through 
to achieve a task - for example, to order a pizza.
With the user journey, it is possible to compare 
experiences across a wide range of users.
We map user journeys to identify and compare the 
highs and lows of individual user’s experiences of 
the same journey.
backText:
Collow the user!
A user journey maps the course a user goes through 
to achieve a task - for example, to order a pizza.
With the user journey, it is possible to compare 
experiences across a wide range of users.
We map user journeys to identify and compare the 
highs and lows of individual user’s experiences of 
the same journey.

frontText:
Capture motivations! 
Identify your user’s pains and gains and discover the 
reasoning behind their decision-making process.
Use the pains and gains to clearly describe the 
value proposition that would matter the most.
Having concretely and concisely visualised pain 
and gains can allow you to effectively identify 
opportunities to address these.
backText:
We recommend that you use a persona at the centre of this method. 
Check out the persona method card if you still need to make one.
Place the relevant persona at the centre of the page.
Brainstorm in a group about this persona’s pains by following 
the template:
a. What makes them angry, anxious, annoyed or afraid? 
b. What obstacles and risks are in their way?
Brainstorm in a group about this persona’s gains:
a. What does this persona expect, need or want? 
b. What would they benefit from?
c. What is their desired outcome?
Identify and highlight the critical pains and gains and how these 
relate to each other.
Consider using this method parallel to an empathy map; together, they can 
create a valuable persona analysis.

frontText:
Put a name to it! 
Personas are archetypes that are used to collect 
common behaviours and attitudes towards a 
product or a service.
These can be an excellent way to compile many 
insights into a manageable object.
backText:
Gather all the insights you want to summarise and inform your 
personas, e.g. interviews, observations, cultural probes, etc.
Cluster and organise insights into similar attitudes and behaviours 
based on the insights gathered through previous methods carried out 
during Observe mode. 
Create personas based on the resulting clusters. Sketch and outline a 
diverse range of personas.
Develop the personas further by thinking about their specific 
goals, behaviours, aspirations, and pain points in and out of the 
relationship with the product or service. Match exact quotes or 
images to each persona.
Name the persona and create a recognisable image to identify them.

frontText:
Find themes and patterns! 
Use affinity diagrams to organise, categorise and 
cluster your insights to find patterns and themes.
Get your entire team to understand your insights in 
the same way. 
This method can help you find empty areas within 
your research where unknowns remain to be 
explored.
backText:
Collect all your insights generated by other methods, such as 
interviews, observations and PEST analysis.
Read and place the insights as post-its on the board, clustering them 
as you go.
Make titles for each group, and feel free to draw arrows and circles 
around subgroups to reveal how the insights link to each other (e.g. 
similarity, dependency or proximity to each other).
Reveal new exciting insights by combining existing ones. You may 
have also identify groups of insights that are underdeveloped, and 
that could be expanded through further research.
Record missing information on differently coloured Post-its and add 
them to the relevant cluster.
Place this map on a whiteboard, wall or digital board. Let the team 
continuously update and revisit the diagram. It will ensure they share 
the mental model of the problem space.

frontText:
Visualize the user experience!
Storyboards are used as a prototype to 
conceptualise an idea in a format similar to a 
comic strip.
Storyboards are powerful when showing an 
interaction between a user and a new product, 
service or IT solution.
In a storyboard, put yourself in the user’s place and 
tell the experience from the user’s point of view.
backText:
Select ideas you would like to prototype through storyboards and 
who should see them. If you choose to present to your manager in the 
organisation, the design will be different than if you present to a user.
Find user journeys if you have made them - they often contain some 
good touch points that can be used to unfold your ideas.
Find the essence of your story by answering three questions: What 
problem does our idea solve, how does it solve it, and what benefits 
does it give the user?
Create a narrative in note form from the user’s point of view that 
describes their journey through your solution - from problems they 
experienced to gained benefits.
Draw 5-10 squares on a large paper and illustrate your story. Start by 
using Post-its so you can swap out drawings and move them around - 
just use line drawings and stick figures.
Make a clean drawing when you finish moving and swapping the 
post-its. Do not spend too much time on the drawing, but make it 
concrete enough for the recipients to understand the concept fully. 
Use speech bubbles, signs and text to support your picture if needed.
Show your storyboard to the selected recipients and use the 
drawing to facilitate a dialogue about the idea and get input on 
how it can be improved.

frontText:
Prototyping in three dimensions!
”Prototypes to decide” are used to test aesthetics, 
functionality and technology considerations.
”Prototypes to decide” can be used throughout 
the development process.
The prototypes should be as simple and 
inexpensive as possible but still allow you to get 
the clarification you need.
backText:
Select one or more ideas for which you want to make a prototype. 
It would help if you prototyped several ideas at once early in the 
development process. Later, you can settle for just one or two when 
the concept is more mature.
Choose which considerations you want to clarify with a prototype: 
look & feel, role or implementation.
• Look & feel clarifies aesthetics, colours, shape, and physical feel.
• Role is about clarifying functions and the functional role of the 
concept for the user.
• Implementation is about clarifying technical feasibility.
Select the resolution you want to make the prototype in. Use quick, 
cheap prototypes early in the project. Prototypes in higher, and thus 
more expensive, resolution only make sense at the end of the project.
Choose whom you want to test the prototype with. Implementation 
prototypes are usually tested internally. Look & feel and role 
prototypes are generally tested with users or external stakeholders.
Build a prototype that suits your choice - search for inspiration for 
techniques on the support sheet.

frontText:
Fake it ‘til you make it! 
Role-playing is an excellent way to prototype a 
product or service implementation. It allows you to 
prototype the process of using the solution.
Role-playing can have many functions: putting 
yourself in the shoes of the user, testing the 
robustness or demonstrating the solution to a 
third party, such as investors.
This is the cheapest and fastest prototype you can 
build, as It is up to you how high fidelity you want 
the environment and props to be.
backText:
Identify the situation you want to focus on and the goal of what 
you want to test with the role-play prototype. Use this to decide on 
scenery (e.g. physical context), roles (e.g. user, employee), and props 
(e.g. product, interfaces, and costumes). 
Create a storyline and as much script, rules and objectives as your 
actors need. Perhaps deliberately introduce misunderstandings? How 
much improvisation you want to allow depends on your solution and 
the prototype’s goal.
Assign roles to volunteers from your design team who will be the 
actors while the others act as the audience. Allow your actors time to 
familiarise themselves with their roles. 
Role-play the scenes and consider recording them for later use and 
analysis.
Discuss the situation with the actors, audience and any external 
guests to gather insights.

frontText:
Digital prototype on paper!
With paper prototypes, you can gain a great 
understanding of how users understand and 
interact with a digital concept or service concept.
Using cardboard, paper and a review of possible 
functionalities, you can easily, cheaply and quickly 
test digital concepts on users.
Paper prototypes encourage the team to become 
very specific about the functionality and structure 
of the solution.
backText:
Collect the necessary materials: cardboard, post-its, paper and pencil.
Create a flowchart describing the features and screens your users 
must go through for each idea you want to prototype.
Draw various screens on cardboard, paper or post-its.
Devise tasks you want the users to try on your prototype, e.g. “Order 
a pizza for a rehearsal room”.
Make routes through the various screens users must go through to 
achieve the goals set for the tasks.
Test the prototype by giving the tasks to the users and having them 
say out loud what they intend to do before pressing the drawn 
button. When they press the right “button”, you give them the next 
screen as a drawing.
Apply insights from your tests to improve the prototype and then 
test again.
Use PowerPoint or POP apps for phones (there are good free ones) to 
make the prototypes more digital. Here you can scan sketches, insert 
pictures and make interactive buttons that change the screens and 
give an experience of a ”real” app.

frontText:
Build a model of the finished product!
A mock-up is a model of a finished product that 
allows the assessment of the design before using 
resources on developing prototypes.
It should simulate the actual product without 
having its complete functionality.
It allows the team to correct mistakes and 
discrepancies early.
backText:
Make a detailed technical description and outline of the final 
product, features, and context based on your chosen ideas.
Build a model of your concept as close to the final concept as possible 
but with cheap materials. If possible, the model must be designed to 
be tested in the final environment and built on a 1:1 scale.
Build a digital or graphical model, if it is a new service, to test essential 
functions and simulate the final service in the real environment.
Pitch your Mock-up to people from different parts of the company 
to provide input and evaluation of the mock-up. It will often 
offer several new ideas for optimising the project and clarify any 
discrepancies that must be addressed.
Test your Mock-up with the users who will use the final concept in 
the environment where it will be sold or used.

frontText:
Define what you are solving! 
Framing your design challenge comprehensively 
will benefit your productivity by narrowing the 
problem and solution space to only what is 
relevant. It will help your team, who will agree 
on a path forward and be able to refer back to a 
common goal.
The design challenge can and should be flexible to 
change as you learn more about the problem and 
redefine your scope.
backText:
Discuss with your team about the insights gathered so far.
With the support of the template, inspire your team with the 
question, “What is the essence of the challenge?“. Write down the 
comments of the team on a whiteboard. Finally, create a common 
sentence starting with “I want to re-design/create the way to…“.
Repeat the previous step with your team by asking, “Who is the 
primary user group? “. The sentence can start with “The main target 
is ... and after that, it also targets... “.
Repeat one last time with the question, “Why is this important? 
What specific facts underpin the challenge? “to create a common 
sentence which follows this structure: “Because right now… and in 
the future… “.
Once the design challenge is defined, use it to discuss and iterate 
until the team is satisfied.
Display the design challenge visibly and accessible to everyone in the 
project. Update it if your scope changes.

frontText:
Let’s be concise! 
As a team, define the goal of the session or project 
in rounds of iteration.
Use this tool to encourage dialogue and align 
team members.
backText:
Divide your team into sub-groups if you have a larger team. This 
exercise works best in small groups of around 3-8 people.
Prepare a common point of departure for all team members. The 
input could be, e.g. project initiation document, a presentation 
from the Product Owner, Problem Owner, Managers etc.; a 
short challenge-brief with information on, e.g. markets, users, 
technological trends, strategic wishes from the organisation, etc. 
Consider that these may require prior reviewing from team members.
Follow the template: write the mission or purpose of the workshop 
or project, the goal or intended outcome of the session, and the 
intended users in 16 words. Give 5 minutes for this step.
Everyone presents their results and has a group discussion to reach 
as much consensus as possible. Encourage people to steal from each 
other for the next step. Alternatively, choose not to perform this step 
and only discuss the results at the end of the exercise instead. Give 
10 minutes for this step.
Repeat steps 3-4 but create an 8-word mission.
Repeat steps 3-4 but create a 4-word mission. You are looking for 4 
most important words of your statement.
Choose the statement that best reflects the team’s mission and write 
it on a large poster or a whiteboard. It will be used as a place to refer 
back to at later stages. A mission statement should be memorable 
and help align the team’s efforts.

frontText:
Hacker, hustler, hipster! 
The successful composition of a team is not only 
the sum of all its members’ capabilities but is the 
result of how these interact with one another. 
Something that is an asset can quickly become a 
point of discomfort within a team due to conflicts, 
competition or redundancies.
Here, we present the simple Hustler, Hipster, 
Hacker framework for developing a team, 
presenting three profiles that must be fulfilled. 
However, to ensure positive interaction between 
the complex personalities and abilities, we 
recommend using the Big 5 framework, for which 
we have a whole other deck of cards for you to use.
backText:
The framework we present here is simple: every team needs a 
Hipster, a Hustler and a Hacker. Let’s take this one step at a time.
Find a Hipster: someone creative such as a designer. Their role is to 
add functional and aesthetic aspects that make the outcome stand out.
Find a Hacker: someone with the technical abilities to develop the 
product. In digital projects, this might be a developer.
Find a Hustler: who delivers the solution to partners and customers. 
They will focus on the business model, marketing and finding 
partnerships.
Consider using this method in parallel with the Big 5 cards. These 
will give you a more thorough understanding of how the team will 
interact and how this may impact your outcomes. Ask us if you want 
to hear about our Big 5 cards; we will happily help you access them.

frontText:
Build the way! 
Once the concept has been well-defined and 
tested, it is time to set implementation milestones 
and actions.
A roadmap is great for communicating the status 
and planned next steps of a project or solution to 
stakeholders. 
Different stakeholders may have unique viewpoints, 
which you translate into necessary actions.
backText:
Decide on the purpose of your roadmap – your main decision is 
whether it is a roadmap for implementation or a solution roadmap, 
which may go many years into the future.
Organise a workshop where you include the central stakeholders 
with the viewpoints and knowledge you need to create a robust and 
valid roadmap.
Draw a suitable timeline on a whiteboard or use the poster from the 
template. This will focus the attention of your participants.
Place key dates, decisions, and activities on Post-its. If it is an 
implementation roadmap, you typically start at the end and work 
backwards. If it is a solution roadmap, you typically start from today 
and work forwards.
Cluster the content into meaningful groups – e.g. swim lanes for 
departments or technologies – anything that makes sense to ease the 
communication of the roadmap. 
Use the roadmap, or parts of it, to communicate with stakeholders 
about the solution or project. Update it regularly through workshops 
to ensure the reliability of the content.

frontText:
Define the value! 
The business model canvas is a strategic and 
tactical management tool for defining a concrete 
and coherent business model for your solution or 
entire business
The canvas is made up of 9 blocks. Each of these 
focuses on one aspect of the business model 
corresponding to the infrastructure, the finances, 
the customers, or the offering.
This tool can help you define areas of your solution 
you had not thought about before and also show 
you how much your solution will require your 
organisation to change and thus mitigate risks.
backText:
Fill out the nine blocks for your solution by starting from the value 
proposition. Down drown in details, write the most important aspects 
of the business model. The template guides you through prompts.
Review all nine blocks once they are filled with the main information. 
Evaluate if something is missing and add it. It helps to take a break 
before doing this or bring a new team member to review your writing.
Check if all the elements on the left-hand side of the canvas support 
the ones on the right, e.g. that customer segments are linked to a 
value proposition. Stay realistic about your solution and your existing 
organisation.
Discuss the canvas with your team and stakeholders in the 
organisation. Especially, make sure that you engage stakeholders 
affected by the changes the business model spells out – e.g. people 
needing to do new activities.
Go deeper and further. Map out alternative business models and 
compare them for viability, or map your competitors’ business 
models and compare them with your own.

frontText:
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities & threats! 
Performing a SWOT analysis can inform your 
strategy for the business or the solution.
The analysis organises positive and negative 
factors of internal and external origin.
A SWOT analysis is simple and easy to do in any 
group size and aligns people.
backText:
Decide on the level of your SWOT analysis – is it, e.g. for your entire 
business or a specific solution?
Organise a workshop where you include the central stakeholders 
with the viewpoints and knowledge you need to create a robust and 
valid SWOT analysis.
Fill out the SWOT template in collaboration. Each of the four spaces 
represents Strengths, Weaknesses (internal), and Opportunities and 
Threats (external).
List internal factors first (Strengths and Weaknesses): 
Strengths - What do we do better than our competitors? What sets 
us apart? What would our competitors point out as our strengths?
Weaknesses - What are we lacking or could improve? What faults 
would our competitors point out? Why are competitors doing better 
than we do?
List external factors second (Opportunities and Threats):
Opportunities – What external circumstances can benefit you if taken 
advantage of? E.g. new technology, changes in policy, etc. 
Threats – What external forces may negatively affect you? These can 
be shifts in the market, technology, industry standards, etc.

frontText:
Explain it to others!
A pitch is a brief presentation of the solution to a 
challenge and is often adapted to the individual 
recipient.
In the pitch, we describe the need, our approach 
to meeting that need, the value we create and 
alternative solutions we compete with.
The pitch must be short enough to be delivered 
informally by the coffee machine, but at the same
time thoroughly conveys the uniqueness of the 
solution.
backText:
Start with the most detailed description of your idea - e.g. a value 
proposition canvas (see card)
Decide who you want to pitch to - each recipient gets their custom pitch.
Assess which values in your solution are the most important to each 
recipient. This is your starting point.
Describe in your pitches these four elements:
• N: The core Needs you have identified
• A: Your Approach to meeting the need
• B: The specific Benefits you create with your approach
• C: The Competing approaches, that your approach differs positively. 
Remember, ”not doing anything” is also a competing alternative.
Use this “fill in the blanks” format as scaffolding for your pitch to 
each recipient:
From [user/situation], we have observed [description of Needs]. 
We address this by [Approach]. 
This provides [user] with [Benefits]. Unlike [Competing alternatives].
Train your pitch in the team and use it to communicate your solution 
to key stakeholders.

frontText:
Regroup and fill in the blanks!
Categories and cluster your ideas so you can 
generate more.
This method can help you find void areas within 
your solution space or ideas that can be further 
developed, or split into multiple ideas or mixed 
with others.
Your ideas can be clustered in many different 
ways, so feel free to use another tool or even 
make up your own.
backText:
Collect all your ideas from a previous brainstorming session.
Read out and cluster the ideas placing them on the whiteboard.
Write titles for each group of ideas.
Draw arrows and circles around subgroups to reveal insights about 
how the ideas link (e.g. similarity, dependency or proximity to each 
other).
Ideate around exciting insights revealed in the previous step.
Identify underdeveloped ideas that could be expanded.
Record new ideas on post-its and add them to the relevant cluster.

frontText:
Trigger your creativity!
Idea association is an effective method of idea 
generation when you lack inspiration or need an 
innovative way of solving a problem.
It breaks the automatic thought patterns to 
solve the task by finding external inspiration for 
new ideas.
Idea association is also used to make the solution 
space bigger and to find more creative solutions. 
Use it when the aim is radical innovation or the 
team is stuck on a solution.
backText:
Choose an image or object that will steer the direction of the ideas. 
Choose either a deliberate direction (e.g. a digital image or object), 
or something random. 
Insert the image or object into the “Inspiration Object” box in the 
template.
Set the timer to 3 minutes and encourage everyone in the team to 
list the associations the object provokes in the “Associations” box. 
Use the question: ”What do you think of when you see the picture?”.
Write your focus in the “Your Focus” box. It can, for example, be 
formulated as a “How Might We?” question or a “Job-to-be-done.”
Brainstorm ideas for solutions based on the associations and your 
focus for the exercise. Try to use all the associations to generate ideas 
that solve your problem.
Share and discuss the ideas that people came up with in the team.

frontText:
Turn it upside down!
Reverse brainstorming flips the problem around 
and generates ideas that answer the reversed 
problem.
This method is proper when the team feels they 
have exhausted all the possibilities within their 
problem space.
backText:
Reverse the problem statement so that you cause the effect you are 
trying to avoid or achieve the opposite effect to the one you intend 
to create, e.g. flip ”How might we make the experience of ordering 
pizza easier for customers” to ”How might we make the experience of 
ordering pizza more difficult for customers”.
Everyone writes and draws their ideas on Post-its, briefly explains 
them to the group and sticks Post-its on the wall or whiteboard.
Generate as many ideas as possible.
Flip and apply the generated ideas to solve the initial problem.

frontText:
Time is ticking!
This quick exercise will challenge the team to 
generate eight ideas per person while under 
the clock.
This method ensures a certain quantity of results.
backText:
Ensure the problem is well defined, e.g. in a ”How-might-we” format.
Give a sheet of paper to each participant and have them fold it in 
half three times (so you have eight different sections).
Explain the rules of this exercise to your team by reading the 
following steps on this card.
Set the timer for 8 minutes.
Each team member sketches one idea per section. These should be 
fast sketches; you have around one minute per idea, so don’t worry 
about making them pretty!
Once the timer goes off, everyone stops drawing.
Share ideas with team members.
Discuss similarities/differences and put the best elements together.

frontText:
Be systematic!
The team members generate ideas individually and 
evaluate and iterate on ideas collectively.
This method ensures everyone’s participation and 
makes your team more efficient in exploring the 
problem space.
The anonymity of the ideas encourages shy 
members and crazy ideas.
backText:
Ensure the design problem is well defined, e.g. in a ”how-might-we” 
format.
Communicate the design brief to your gathered team.
Choose one person to be the moderator.
Generate as many ideas as possible individually, and draw them on 
post-its for 15 min.
The moderator gathers all the post-its, shuffles them and randomly 
redistributes them to the participants.
Each participant reads out the ideas given to them while the 
moderator maps out the ideas on the whiteboard and clusters them 
based on recurring topics. 
Participants discuss what they like about the ideas.
Everyone votes on the ideas to find the most interesting proposals.

frontText:
Steal with pride! 
Find inspiration for idea creation by looking for 
existing solutions within your organisation, other 
industries or sectors.
Use the most relevant elements from these 
existing solutions as inspiration and mix them.
A solution widely known in one field can be a source 
of great innovation when used in another context.
backText:
Choose a direction for your ideation, e.g. in the form of a design 
question or a mood board.
List (by each team member individually) existing solutions that can 
potentially solve the design question or maybe a part of it. Think 
outside your field, industry, and business.
Create a joint list with the top 1-2 solutions from each team 
member’s list.
Research the solutions more closely and prepare a 3 min 
Lightning Demo:
Hint: to make a long story short, try to explain it like this: ”It’s kind of 
like ... [something we know], but [the important difference]”.
Pitch your solutions to each team member and outline the ideas, 
elements or principles that seem worthwhile from each solution on a 
large whiteboard.
Combine whiteboard content to create solution concepts 
collaboratively, guided by your design questions.

frontText:
Let it rain!
Brainstorming is the quintessential method for 
ideation.
Once the problem space has been framed, the 
team suggests solutions.
All points of view and ideas are welcome at this 
stage, however crazy or out-there.
backText:
Ensure the problem is well defined, e.g. in a “how-might-we” design 
question format (see card).
Write down the design question on a whiteboard or Post-it and 
communicate it to your gathered team.
Explain the brainstorming rules to everyone:
• Don’t judge ideas!
• Build on others’ ideas!
• Welcome crazy ideas!
• Remember the design question or brief.
• Go for quantity!
Encourage each person to write and draw their ideas on post-its, 
briefly explain them to the group and stick them on the wall or 
whiteboard.
Generate as many ideas as possible.

frontText:
Evaluate the ideas!
This method is used to select the best ideas 
based on requirements created from your data. It 
assesses ideas together as a team.
Often, a natural dialogue arises among the team 
about the choice of requirements and how the 
ideas fit. This discussion is at least as important as 
defining requirements themselves.
This tool is typically used to filter, discuss and 
prioritise well-defined ideas from various idea 
generation activities.
backText:
Spread out all your data on a wall or a large table. Include all your 
ideas from the idea creation process. 
Establish 3-5 critical requirements for whether an idea is a good or 
bad solution by looking through all your data. Consider user needs, 
technological feasibility and business viability.
Write the requirements on the right end of the dashed lines (one per 
line) so that the most crucial need (i.e. what must be fulfilled) is at 
the top of the funnel.
Write one idea on each Post-it, and place them at the top of your 
”idea funnel” poster.
Discuss each idea. If it meets the requirements, move it down 
through the funnel. Ideas that reach the bottom meet all 
requirements and are approved.
Discuss rejected ideas on top of the funnel. Try to change them to 
meet the requirements. 
Park ideas that cannot be evaluated in the parking lot. Later research 
to approve or reject them.
Select and prototype a few approved ideas as different from each 
other as possible.

frontText:
Live it to see it! 
Immerse yourself into a community or someone 
else’s life and uncover an inside view. It could 
mean shadowing a person for a while, observing 
how they perform their daily tasks, and even 
arranging a homestay.
Immersion can be beneficial to understand 
someone else without making assumptions or 
falling into stereotypes or biases.
backText:
Evaluate how much involvement could be beneficial and for how 
long. Depending on the project, shadowing someone at work might 
be enough, whereas a homestay could provide valuable insight for 
others.
Observe and record as much as possible once you are in the setting—
record observations as objectively as possible. Pure observations are 
more comparable with other team members’ observations, including 
direct quotes, images or video recordings. However, if you have 
exciting reflections, record them separately, as they are helpful later.
Ask clarifying questions while you shadow someone about the 
task they are carrying out, why they are doing it that way, how 
they decide to do them, etc. Make them feel comfortable so your 
presence’s effect on their behaviour is minimal.
Analyse and find patterns within your data alongside data from other 
team members’ observations once you return.

frontText:
Ask around! 
Group interviews or focus groups give deep 
insights about a topic. Not only do you get 
different views on one topic, but you can hear 
where their perspectives differ and what they 
agree on.
The interview subjects can be selected and 
grouped for a particular purpose. If you interview 
a group of co-workers in a similar role, you will 
understand their joint experience deeply. In 
contrast, if they work in different roles, you will 
uncover deep insights into what is shared or not 
among them.
Remember that this method may present complex 
group dynamics affecting the outcome.
backText:
Write an interview guide containing the prompts or questions you 
will ask.
Collect relevant test subjects.
Describe a task the test subjects should try to achieve.
Record the session on video since non-verbal cues such as facial 
expressions tell much about the users’ feelings.
Facilitate a discussion between the participants with the prompts in 
your interview guide. Start with an open-ended discussion around 
the topic, where you only moderate the debate and ask in-depth 
questions. Then address the themes your team is interested in 
exploring from the interview guide. Depending on the tasks and your 
goal, you can include a test of a product.
Gather and evaluate all the material together after you have covered 
the topics in your interview guide. Use another method for this, such 
as an affinity diagram (see card).

frontText:
Provoke a user! 
Provotypes provoke a reaction and deep 
dialogue with the test subject – a user, expert, or 
stakeholder in the project.
These are often extreme solutions that we present 
to a person so the test subject briefly thinks it is 
the actual solution.
We use provotypes to gain insight into attitudes to, 
e.g. new technologies and radically new solutions.
backText:
Prepare a sound recorder and a notebook to record your insights.
Discuss within the team what you would like the reaction to be - and 
who you would like the response from. Select specific people you 
want to test the provotype with.
Make low-fidelity provotypes (preferably several) that will cause the 
user to respond thoughtfully to the idea - e.g. mock-up of a website, 
a brochure, or a product description on a web shop.
Plan how to collect data from the provotype test. Using the Rapid 
Feedback Matrix is often a good idea (see card). 
Present the provotype to your test subject, e.g. tell them you are 
looking for the best way to implement your new concept.
Let users try some different provotypes and give feedback. When 
one arouses interest, ask for details - What will it mean for users in 
their daily life? What benefits do they see? What disadvantages? 
Repeatedly ask why to explore the motivation behind it.
Collect feedback in the matrix’s four fields (see Rapid Feedback 
Matrix card), and record the interview to get all the details.
Finalise the provotyping tests. Collect test results, e.g., rapid feedback 
matrices, quotes from test subjects and situational images from the 
test site, and find insights that you can use to inspire a good design.

frontText:
Look into the system! 
PEST stands for political, economic, social and 
technological. It provides a comprehensive 
structure to analyse the external context around a 
solution or situation.
No solution is developed in a vacuum. External 
forces will affect how a solution is received and 
adopted. Understanding these forces allows you to 
predict and meet unexpected needs and risks.
PEST analysis can be used to inform long-term 
strategic planning.
backText:
Explore broadly what to include in your analysis for every step. 
Consider the level of potential impact, the time frame (from 
immediate to long term), positive or negative impacts, whether this 
impact will increase or decrease over time, etc.
Analyse the political environment. Identify policies, guidelines, 
political relationships, etc., that could impact your solution. Explore 
the local, regional, national and international landscape. Consider, 
e.g. elections and national priorities.
Analyse the economic factors that may affect your venture. E.g. 
general aspects such as gross domestic product, unemployment 
rate, credit availability and interest rates, inflation, etc. Analyse the 
economic situation of your potential users/customers.
Analyse the socio-cultural factors that may impact your market. 
Understand how user needs are shaped and anticipate shifts in 
culture and society. Evaluate your user’s attitudes through, e.g. market 
and cultural trends, demographic and age distribution, values, etc.
Analyse the technological impact on your business solution. 
Consider what new technologies, products and services are being 
developed or introduced to the market, the life-cycle of current 
technology, what the current technological spending budget is, etc.
This method can be extended to PESTEL buy adding Environmental 
and Legal factors.

frontText:
Understand deeper! 
Cultural probes or diary studies help you 
understand your user’s daily needs, values and 
challenges.
For extended periods, ask the user to collect their 
experiences using an individual probe or set of 
analogue or digital probes, e.g. a diary, camera, 
postcard, map, etc. You will benefit from a deeper 
and more unbiased reflection of the user’s daily 
life and self-documentation.
Cultural probes collect information without you
backText:
Choose what you want to explore: How would you use the 
information you collect from this method? Would you make, e.g. 
empathy maps, user journey maps, personas, etc?
Define whom you need as research participants and how many of 
them to get meaningful results.
Decide what ways of self-documenting would be most appropriate: 
diaries kept over however long is relevant (a day, a week, or even 
years), taking photos, audio or video recordings of a task performed 
and its context with their phone or a disposable camera, mapping 
out elements of a system or journeys, entries in a blog?
Write instructions for the tasks and the timeframe you want 
participants to complete. Instruct them directly and simply, as you 
cannot see how they perform the tasks and correct them. Therefore, 
test your instructions beforehand. Include your contact info in case of 
questions or doubts.
Give/send a cultural probe package with task instructions to 
participants to perform and self-document. Make it pleasant to carry 
out the tasks and interact with the probes. Even consider incentives. 
Receive back the probes. Analyse and cluster them to find patterns. 
Follow up with interviews to deepen your insights.

frontText:
Get energised!
This is a version of brainstorming to warm up or 
increase your team’s energy.
This can also be used as an ice-breaker tool when 
the participants do not know each other, e.g. in 
co-creation sessions.
The team members pass an object amongst each 
other and take turns generating ideas.
This method facilitates the association of ideas 
between participants in a team.
backText:
Find a room where all participants can sit in a circle. Bring your team 
together and communicate the brainstorming topic.
Find an object that can be quickly passed and thrown around. Don’t 
use anything sharp, heavy or valuable!
Explain the exercise (you can read this section of the card).
Have one moderator that records the ideas on paper.
Throw the object to one team member, have them shout an idea, 
and pass it on to another person in the circle.
Repeat this, at least until everyone has participated.

frontText:
Put it down on a whiteboard! 
Create a shared space between your team to 
combine all your ideas and insights in real-time.
This activity can benefit various activities in 
facilitating alignment between participants and 
inspiring new associations.
Problem mapping can energise team members 
by allowing them to add their input easily and 
creating an opportunity for casual interaction.
backText:
Choose your tool. It can be a physical whiteboard, flip-over, or a 
virtual whiteboarding tool.
Set the purpose of the session and encourage people to participate in 
drawing the map.
List the actors involved on the left side of your board – keep it simple, 
no more than 8.
Write a goal on the right that you all agree on – imagine it as the 
ending of your story.
Draw boxes and arrows that connects left and right side. Boxes are 
concrete activities or events needed for the actors to deliver the goal. 
Keep it simple. No more than 15 boxes with activities.
Discuss the map in the group and use it e.g., to choose focus points 
for your next steps.

frontText:
Build an ideal solution to a problem! 
Lego® Serious play® is a framework to work 
together in building models and get the whole 
team involved in development.
It’s a group tool to build and create dialogue, 
strategies and new solutions. It teaches introverts 
and extroverts—to think with their hands and 
better communicate their ideas, allowing a greater 
flow of information.
This method helps the group to create 3D 
elements together. It fosters creativity and involves 
more significant details.
It aligns the group by creating a joined focus and a 
memory of what they are building.
backText:
Remember Lego® Serious play® ground rules and build the ideal solution to 
your problem.
Explain that the exercise aims to create a new service or product. It 
does not exist yet, so let your ideas flow freely and enjoy the process. 
Everybody builds 3 solutions in 10 minutes. Use all the bricks you 
want for this.
Each person presents their solution to the group once the time 
has passed.
Each person builds a single joined grand solution in 10 minutes.
Each participant prepares a presentation of their model. The 
presentation method is up to them, but they must include their model.
Everyone presents their model in turn to get rapid feedback.
Discuss the feedback in the group for 5 minutes.
Add and adjust the model as needed for another 5 minutes

frontText:
Stay alert! 
Everyone must be placed in a circle and think fast 
and strategically in this energiser. You want to be 
the last ninja standing.
Wake up and engage your team with this fastpaced exercise.
Use this tool to break the ice or as an energiser.
backText:
This exercise works best with a group of approx. 10 participants, so 
divide if there are more participants than that. Have everyone sit in 
a circle.
To begin, everyone shouts ”Ninja!” and freezes in a ninja position. 
Choose one person to be the first attacker. Ask everyone to 
remember who was before and after them, as the turns will go 
clockwise, but the game requires people to move around.
The attacker begins the game. The aim is to be the last ninja standing. 
When it is your turn, you are only allowed one smooth motion: either 
use it to move away or hit another player’s hand. If hit, you are out of 
the game.
The attacker’s turn ends when they miss. The person that was on 
their right then becomes the attacker.
The last one still in the game wins.

frontText:
Warm up LSP! 
Lego® Serious play® is a framework to work 
together in building models and get the whole 
team involved in development.
It’s a group tool to build and create dialogue, 
strategies and new solutions. It teaches introverts 
and extroverts to think with their hands and better 
communicate their ideas, allowing a greater flow 
of information.
This method helps the group to create 3D 
elements together. It fosters creativity and involves 
more significant details.
It aligns the group by creating a joined focus and a 
memory of what they are building.
backText:
LEGO serous play ground rules: everybody builds and share, every story is 
equal, it’s YOUR opinion embedded in the model, explore the model NOT 
the interpretation, elaborate on the underlined story, if you don’t know 
what you want to build, start building the answer will reveal itself, there is 
no RIGHT WAY to build!
Warm up 1: Build Animals
Build as many animals as you can in 20 minutes. Use all the bricks 
you want. One brick can represent an animal if the participants have 
a story or thought behind it.
After the building session, every participant must present their 
animals and what they can do or the thought behind them. Have a 
prize for the winner – maybe something that can be shared.
Warm up 2: Build a Duck vs Draw a Duck 
Half of the group gets handed Lego bricks to build a duck. The 
other half is instructed to draw LEGO ducks (have a model of a duck 
prepared for inspiration).
Have them build as many versions as they can think of. Every time 
they have a new model, they must add a line on a piece of paper to 
keep count. Instruct the building group that it’s a new duck every 
time they move a brick or add it to an already-made model.
Note: It is faster to modify a built model than a drawing, making it faster 
(often by a factor of 7) to produce new ideas together.

frontText:
Create a common outcome! 
Brainwalking is a collaborative brainstorming 
method that gets people moving and thinking 
creatively. Participants move around the room and 
collaborate by building on others’ ideas.
Encourage participation of all team members in 
one outcome to reinforce a sense of cohesion and 
to allow participants to have fun together. It helps 
energise the group and makes them more open to 
sharing their ideas.
This can be used as a productive brainstorming 
method and a tool to align participants, energise
the room and break the ice.
backText:
Everyone illustrates an idea by writing, drawing on flip-chart paper, 
and hanging it on a wall. It is done individually or in groups.
In 1-2 min rounds, participants rotate to the following flip-chart 
paper and further develop the other person’s idea or develop new 
ideas based on it.
The exercise ends when everyone has made a complete circle 
around all the flip-chart papers. You can then discuss the outcomes 
as a team.

frontText:
Share with the group!
This method is used to get detailed feedback on 
a mature prototype from user segments we are 
particularly interested in.
The solution is presented to a small group 
representing the central target group.
The focus group test helps us determine how much 
value the individual features in the product create 
for the users in different segments. We discover 
how to adapt the final but significant details before 
a possible product launch.
backText:
Build a high-fidelity prototype of the solution, e.g. minimum viable 
product or early software. All the features you want to test are 
included. Ideally, you want a prototype that is so mature that it could 
be launched but only includes the most critical functions.
Fill out test cards (see card) with the hypotheses you are testing and 
decide how to gather information, i.e. what questions will answer 
those hypotheses.
Segment your test subjects. E.g., first movers and early followers who 
will be the first to embrace the solution and some who represent 
the vast majority, i.e. the early and late majority. Ensure a good 
distribution of the segments and formulate tasks for each. 
Present the prototypes and the task description to your test subject 
without additional help and let them use your solution.
Facilitate discussions with and between the focus group members 
about the tasks and what problems they faced. Ask in-depth 
questions and ensure to address the themes and questions your 
team wrote on the test cards.
Record the session on video as non-verbal cues such as facial 
expressions tell much about the users’ feelings.
Evaluate the material from the finished tests one task at a time and 
improve your design.

frontText:
Put your action where your mouth is!
This method is typically used to assess how much 
users like a solution and whether it makes sense to 
proceed with it.
An action test determines if a solution provides 
enough value to the user for them to invest 
time or money in it. e.g., buying the product, 
downloading the app, or signing up for something 
that takes time.
This test helps quantify how much the user likes 
the solution and provides insight into people’s 
willingness to pay.
backText:
Build a medium to high-fidelity prototype of the solution you want 
to test, e.g. fake door, relabel, brochure, or a physical model. Test 
subjects should believe your solution exists when they act., i.e., 
purchase, download or register.
Find a test location (physical or digital) with numerous relevant users 
where the prototype appears credible and where you can monitor 
the decisions your test subjects make.
Present the prototypes to your users, or let them present 
themselves. Assign different costs to your test subjects to identify 
their willingness to pay. E.g. give them different prices or ask for 
different amounts of time commitment.
Record as much data as possible when the test subject takes action, 
e.g., video or screen recording, to capture factors that affect the test 
subjects’ decisions.
Finalise the tests by analysing your material, e.g. user quotes and 
situational images from the test site and, most importantly, the 
data on willingness to take action. Use this to inform transactional 
features, e.g. target price, time commitment, and value proposition.

frontText:
Time will tell!
Testing in a living lab and a 100-day test are similar 
methods. In both, a prototype is tested over a long 
period in an environment as similar as possible to 
the one in which the final product will be used. 
This method tests whether the solution creates 
the value we expect for the ones we expect. It 
uncovers what users and your business gain using 
or owning your solution.
Testing like this can clarify technical assumptions 
– e.g., product robustness in real-use situations, 
over a period of time.
backText:
Build a high-fidelity prototype of the solution, e.g. minimum viable 
product or early software. All the features you want to test need to 
be included.
Clarify what you want to learn from the test – use, e.g. test cards or 
assumption dump (see cards). 
Segment your test subjects. E.g., first movers and early followers who 
will be the first to embrace the solution and some who represent 
the vast majority, i.e. the early and late majority. Ensure a good 
distribution of the segments and formulate tasks for each. 
Prepare your data collection approach. You need qualitative and 
quantitative data with minimal interference from the test subject. 
Techniques include text message questions, online surveys, 
automated data collection, observations, and interviews (see cards).
Present the prototype and task description to your users. Also, 
instruct them on how you will get data from them throughout and 
after the test. 
Evaluate all gathered material after the test. Summarise quantitative 
data in graphs and figures. Compile qualitative data as aggregated 
insights and supporting images. Organise a learning workshop with 
your team to elicit learnings and refine the design.

frontText:
Test the “out-there” solution!
This method is used early or in the middle of a 
project to ensure that we search the solution 
space broadly. We should not sacrifice radically 
new solutions in favour of the obvious ones.
The goal of the project can often be unclear. 
Testing one prototype can help narrow the goal. 
But, By testing both the obvious and the far-fromobvious prototypes, we illuminate a much larger 
solution space. 
We do dark-horse testing by consciously testing 
the opposite of the solution we all agree is the safe
