choice – the consensus solution.
backText:
Start by making a fast and cheap prototype of one of your most 
radical ideas, e.g. in the form of wireframes, prototyping on paper, 
brochures, or storyboards. Also, prototype the consensus idea you 
want to challenge with the Dark Horse.
Collect your entire team and relevant test subjects without 
overwhelming the test subjects.
Present the prototype to your test subject and let them use it. 
Afterwards, you test your consensus idea with the user and ask them 
to compare them.
Record as much as possible through video and pictures and use the 
Rapid Feedback Matrix (see card) to structure the insights. Emphasise 
the reflection fields, i.e., what questions came up during the test, and 
which ideas for solutions and features emerged. 
Finalise the test by using your new insights to challenge and redesign 
your consensus idea in the team. Use the recordings to remind you 
about the inspirational details that the Dark Horse brought to light.

frontText:
Start with the foundations! 
The result of a house of quality is a common 
visualisation that shows the considerations of the 
entire project team. In the light of user/customer 
requirements.
The tool integrates customer needs and concerns, 
technical requirements, how the solution 
compares with those of competitors and trade-offs 
between these.
This method uses a set of helps you prioritise 
requirements and considerations while 
maintaining a cohesive common plan and design.
backText:
Collect existing user insights gathered through focus groups, 
provotyping, testing etc.
Elicit Customer Attributes (CAs). These are phrases customers use 
to describe the product, e.g. “easy to open“. Customers may not 
necessarily be just end-users, so consider, e.g. sellers, regulators, etc.
Bundle CAs representing user concerns in groups. It is often beneficial 
to agree on these with the entire project team.
Prioritise CAs and give a “relative importance“ score. You can do this in 
several ways, e.g. based on quantitative survey data.
Evaluate each CA on customer perception of your product’s 
performance against your competitors.
Sort out engineering characteristics (ECs). These technical factors, e.g. 
“seal resistance”, are derived from the CAs.
Fill out the “relationship matrix” indicating how much each EC affects 
each CA. You can define the relevant scale. Remember to differentiate 
between negative and positive impacts.
Establish objective measures for each EC in the appropriate units for 
your product and competing ones. You can also set target values.
Use the roof matrix to display trade-offs and positive and negative 
interactions between ECs, e.g. increasing size negatively affects weight.

frontText:
Saying, doing, thinking, feeling! 
Empathy map allows you to collect insights about 
the user’s behaviours and attitudes in one place so 
the team has a common understanding.
Your team will build empathy with your users 
through creating empathy maps.
Empathy map breaks down what the user says, 
does, thinks, and feels. Here you can use insights 
from other methods, such as interviews for what 
they say, observation for what they do, etc.
backText:
We recommend that you use a persona at the centre of this method. 
Check out the persona method card if you still need to make one.
Choose a persona for which you want to create an empathy map.
Place them at the centre of the page.
Look at four quadrants in the template. Each quadrant represents 
what the user says, thinks, does and feels.
List what the user says. Ideally, use direct quotes from interviews, 
focus groups, tests such as think-out-loud tests, etc.
Write what the user thinks. Try to understand and share the user’s 
feelings behind their words. Why were they saying it, e.g. was it to be 
polite, because they were unsure, ashamed, afraid?
Draw/Describe the user’s actions and behaviours. What do they do, 
and how? Use insights from observation, cultural probes, etc.
Describe the user’s feelings. List positive and negative emotions and 
briefly describe what causes them.
Find the exciting insights in the interaction among the empathy map’s 
quadrants: Are they overlapping? Do they contradict one another? 
If one of the quadrants needs more data, you might want to go back and 
research further through the appropriate method.

frontText:
Find a visual direction 
Mood boards create visual inspiration and 
direction for later developing ideas and concepts.
Mood boards increase an overall understanding 
and perception of users’ desires towards the 
solution. They capture what is challenging 
to express in words, such as aesthetics and 
atmosphere.
Mood boards can be used as a powerful method 
to convey a desired design direction without the 
recipient getting lost in the details and, therefore, 
relate more freely to the visual vision of the final 
solution.
backText:
Find a variety of materials that you can use for your mood boards. 
These may be newspapers, magazines, online images (printed), 
drawings/sketches, paints/colours and cutouts of words/phrases. 
Find glue, markers, tape, and large posters (e.g., flip-overs).
Sketch or write down keywords matching the data you collected on 
users’ desires and needs.
Find elements in your material that best convey the users’ wishes. 
Try to communicate aesthetics and other desires. Attach items to the 
poster or flip-over with tape so you can move them around.
Present your mood boards to the group. Use various mood boards to 
agree on the cores of the user’s desires and needs.
Take a picture of each mood board.
Create a common mood board by combining items from the 
individual mood boards. More visuals can be added as this part of the 
process is often the start of a new common visual understanding of 
the concept’s direction.
Present the overall mood board in a short pitch to users or use it 
internally to communicate users’ desires and needs visually.

frontText:
Visualise who is involved! 
A stakeholder map can be a great way to visualise 
key stakeholders involved in the project and the 
relationships between them.
The resulting visualisation can be used as a 
reference for the team and updated as you 
uncover new information. It can inspire new 
opportunities or help gather complex information.
You can show the relationships between the 
stakeholders in terms of financial, material, 
and information flows, among other relevant 
information.
backText:
Collect all the insights you need to create the map: who is involved 
and what they provide to each other. Consider co-creating this map 
with someone familiar with the project or problem and the flow 
between the stakeholders involved.
Prepare a whiteboard to create and iterate the map quickly.
List all the relevant stakeholders on individual post-its.
Place key stakeholders on the matrix described in our template. The 
two axes will help you organise the stakeholders by influence and 
interest levels.
Draw connections between them that describe financial, material 
and information flow amongst them. Add any other flows relevant to 
your project or problem to complete the map.

frontText:
Dig a little deeper! 
The fishbone diagram is a helpful method to 
analyse the root causes of a given challenge.
The outcome of this method is a visual 
representation of cause and effect consisting 
of a se of factors branching off from the root, 
appearing like a fishbone.
backText:
Identify an appropriate problem statement (i.e. the “effect”) and write 
it down at the head of the fish within the diagram (see template).
Find the main categories of underlying factors that may cause 
the “effect”. Often the following categories are helpful: materials, 
equipment, methods, measurement, environment, and people.
Uncover why this “effect” happens and write them as subcategories 
of the main branches. Some may belong to multiple categories.
Ask why repeatedly to break down causes and sub-causes further.

frontText:
Test the waters! 
A service pilot is a prototype of a service or a 
part of a service. It allows you to test your design 
choices before fully delivering it.
In a service pilot, you attempt to replicate as 
many of the service’s touchpoints as possible and 
relevant to the highest level of fidelity.
backText:
Collect any lower-fidelity prototypes or concept specifications that 
you may have of the service. 
Examine the service you have conceptualised, ideally as a service 
blueprint.
Select the touchpoints you want to get feedback on and those 
essential to testing other steps in the process.
Consider replacing some components with alternatives requiring 
fewer resources. For example, you may want to try lower-fidelity 
prototypes of the products that the user interacts with throughout 
the service, such as an app, a device, etc.
Launch the pilot for a limited time at the location and with the user 
type as close to the final ones as possible.
Gather valuable insights and use them to improve your design.

frontText:
Do the bare minimum! 
A minimum viable product (MVP) is a concept 
that originated in Lean Start-Up. The idea is to 
create the product version with only the necessary 
features to measure customer reactions. MVP has 
the core functionality, which can be expanded later.
You can test the customer’s actual behaviour 
towards the product with an MVP, with minimal 
investment of money and time.
What an MVP must include will depend on your 
concept, resources, etc. Ask yourself what you can 
remove while keeping the core functiona
backText:
Gather relevant documentation from your design research, e.g. user 
journeys, jobs to be done, pains and gains, etc.
Plan a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) carefully to avoid wasting 
resources: Analyse all your design research and test results to elicit 
the functionality valuable to the users and your business.
Decide how you will measure the performance of your MVP when 
deployed, and use this to prioritise functionality. 
(see the Test Cards card)
List and prioritise all the features needed for the essential 
functionality. A popular way to map them is a 2x2 matrix based on 
impact and an urgency axis. Include high-impact and high-urgency 
features. Include core features for the business model. Discard 
features you can add later. Iterate until the number of features can be 
achieved within your time and budget.
Build the MVP by organising features into Agile Sprints. Our Agile 
Planning card in the “Understand“ mode can help you do this.

frontText:
If a picture is worth a thousand words, then a 
video is worth a million! 
Video prototypes are compelling to get customer 
feedback when you want the focus on the concept 
or look rather than the specific functionality.
It is an excellent prototyping method for service 
concepts.
It is a fast and cheap prototype to make and test.
Make the video as beautiful as possible. The 
feedback and all user attention should be on the 
concept, not the video itself.
backText:
Find the equipment you need to record and edit video (e.g. camera, 
video editing software).
Draw a storyboard for the video: choose a style and what aspects 
of the concept or idea you want to portray. Use our storyboard 
template here.
List what shots you want to film and write a final script if necessary. 
List resources you need: people, permits, cameras, etc.
Shoot the video. Ensure you have: the equipment, storyboard, list of 
shots, and script.
Edit all your collected footage to create the final video. Add text and 
effects to enhance your message.
Show your video prototype to gather feedback or illustrate the 
concept to potential customers, users, investors or partners.

frontText:
Visualise your service! 
A service blueprint visualises a service’s 
components: people, processes, artefacts, etc.
Similarly to a user journey, it maps out the 
touchpoints between the service and the 
customer. However, service blueprints display the 
components that help deliver the service but are 
hidden from the customer.
A complete picture of the process allows you 
to find missing elements, reduce redundancies, 
create new bridges between processes or people 
or identify opportunities to improve the service.
backText:
Bring a user journey to the workshop. It is a good starting point for a 
service blueprint.
Draw a diagram of the customer’s steps and decisions to achieve a 
goal. Map it from the beginning to the end of the service process. If 
we, e.g. create a pizza delivery service, a step would be calling the 
store to order a pizza.
Add activities visible to the customer: interactions between the 
customer and a person or an artefact (e.g., computer, app, ATM). In 
our example, you would add: employee answers the phone and takes 
the pizza order.
Map backstage actions an employee performs that support the 
visible ones. In our example, this could be an employee entering the 
pizza order into a computer system.
Add process steps that must occur for the service to succeed. E.g., 
credit card validation can be added to our pizza service example.
Add any metrics that detail relevant information, such as user 
feedback in the form of emotions at each stage, the time each step 
takes or their cost. Use these to make informed changes to your 
service design.

frontText:
Find what you need! 
By going through the process defined in this 
methodology, you will be able to determine where 
you are, what you want to achieve and the steps to 
get there.
Gathering all this information in a poster form will 
create a common frame for your team to reference 
and update.
backText:
Participants fill out the template together, as a poster. Start with 
describing the challenge - is the project a re-design or new design, 
who are the target groups, and what facts support the project?
Define your goal - What level of innovation are you aiming for, what 
are your concrete sub-goals, and what value do you expect to create?
Describe your Design Vision by gathering your challenge and goal 
into a memorable map, narrative or pitch.
Describe the team - what are each member’s superpowers and 
kryptonite? Consider both professional and personal aspects.
Describe your current situation - What are your existing knowledge 
and assumptions about the challenge?
Compare the team and situation (left column) with the challenge 
and goal you defined (right column) to determine the Knowledge 
Gap. Be as specific as possible but realise that you may need more 
information to engage precisely with some gaps.
Finally, give your project a catchy title.
Update this template regularly as the team goes through the design 
process to reflect the evolution of the project.

frontText:
Plan flexibly! 
Agile processes organise tasks within time-bound 
self-contained sprints, by the end of which 
features are ready to be rolled out and tested.
Agile planning is based on user stories which 
are assigned to sprints. Tasks are not defined by 
technical specifications but rather by users’ needs. 
User stories can be grouped to form an epic.
An agile plan is flexible to constant iterations. 
Completed sprints allow learning and help plan the 
tasks and structure the next ones.
backText:
List the user stories or epics to be solved for the release.
Score them in terms of priority and size. Discuss any discrepancies 
and agree on a final assessment of these criteria.
Create a sprint and assign stories to it. Decide on the length of sprints 
for your team. They usually take 1-4 weeks. Once one sprint is full, 
create another one and repeat this until all user stories are placed.
At the start of every sprint, have a meeting to discuss learnings from 
previous sprints and to iterate the plan accordingly. Changes can 
include timings, prioritisation, new features, etc. Use this meeting to 
detail user stories further, break these down into specific tasks, and 
assign these to particular team members.
Place the post-its describing user stories, tasks and whom they are 
assigned to on a Kanban board that is visible to everyone (physically 
or digitally). The tasks should initially be under the “backlog” column 
on the left. As items get tackled, the team should move them across 
the board through “to do” and “in progress“ until they are placed 
under “completed“. You can personalise the columns of the board.
Hold a stand-up meeting at the start of every day where everyone 
shares their progress from the previous day, what they will tackle on 
that day and mention any obstacles they have encountered. These 
should take up to 15 minutes.

frontText:
Be concise and visualise! 
The story behind “The Back of a Napkin” is that you 
are at a dinner meeting. Suddenly, you discover 
that person sitting next to you has the capacity and 
interest to help you fund a big new solution you are 
working on. But you have around two minutes to 
get them on board. All you have at hand to explain 
your idea is a dinner napkin and a pencil.
This technique shows that thinking in pictures can 
help anyone to get new ideas and to communicate 
them in simple lines.
This can be used as an alignment tool for the team.
backText:
The team uses folded pieces of A4 paper (or an A5 sheet) as napkins. You 
can use simple sketching techniques such as stick figures, squares, circles, 
triangles, etc. You can use a few words, but words cannot be the primary 
communication tool on the napkin.
Look at examples of both of these exercises in the templates.
Napkin 1: The Problem Napkin
Each person must take 10 minutes to draw their perception of the 
problem on their “napkin”. It includes the who, how much and why 
of the problem at hand.
Use 10 min for each member to present their napkin to the group.
Create a common group napkin with the collected inspiration from 
all the napkins.
Napkin 2: The Solution Napkin 
Each person must take 10 min to draw their solution to the problem 
on their “napkin”. It includes answering at least 3 questions about 
who or what, where, when and how.
Use 10 min for each member to present their napkin to the group.
Create a common group napkin with the collected inspiration from 
all the napkins.

frontText:
Voice of the customer! 
Communicate what you want to be developed 
in the customer’s voice instead of with detailed 
specifications – what do you want to enable the 
user to do? 
The user story map consists of your entire solution, 
broken down into short and concrete user stories. 
Use the user story map to continuously prioritise 
which features to develop next and what to 
include in your product launches.
backText:
Formulate a high-level user story for each key feature your final 
solution should include and place them under a phase or process 
step in the user story map template. A user story typically follows 
this format:
“As a [user persona], I want [action or feature] so that [benefit or goal].” 
E.g., “As a website visitor, I want to easily find pricing information so 
that I can make an informed purchasing decision.”
Review your high-level user story map with the development/project 
team. Together you will now break all your high-level user stories into 
many detailed ones. 
Prioritise user stories jointly by moving the user stories on the 
template. Select a coherent amount of high-priority stories to be 
developed first – this will be your MVP1 – but ensure it can be 
deployed as a value-creating solution. 
Define acceptance criteria for all the detailed user stories in close 
collaboration with the development team. There are different 
acceptance criteria each user story must meet depending on the 
need: functional, performance, usability acceptance criteria, etc. 
These will tell you when a user story is completed or not.

frontText:
Achieve Product-Market fit! 
A value proposition canvas helps you visualise the 
value you create for your customers.
A product or service’s success relies on its ability 
and effectiveness in relieving pains or creating 
customer gains.
The value proposition canvas expands on the value 
proposition block of the business model canvas.
backText:
Gather all information you have on user needs across different 
segments. Also, gather all your information on the benefits created 
by your conceptual solution.
Fill out the right side of the template first – this is the customer/user 
perspective: Place a relevant customer persona at the centre. List the 
jobs that the persona is trying to get done. List what pains the user 
experiences and what gains they expect or desire (see also the Pains 
and Gains card).
Fill out the left side of the template second. List the core features 
of your solution in the “Products & Services“ section. List how the 
solution relieves the pains listed in the circle. List how the solution 
fulfils gains.
Repeat this for each of your customer/user segments and assess the 
product market fit by comparing how your solution creates value for 
each segment. 
Finally, define early indicators that point to whether your solution 
will achieve its intended goal. Early indicators are metrics that can be 
monitored throughout the development process.

frontText:
No-waste business model! 
The lean canvas is an adaption of the classic 
business model canvas. It follows a similar structure 
but combines it with the Lean methodology to 
achieve a “quick to market” model.
The Lean Canvas guides you through 9 blocks 
detailing your business model and go-to-market 
approach.
backText:
Fill out the Customer Segment block on the template. Detail who it is 
you are solving a problem for with your solution.
Fill out the Problem block. List the 1-3 most important problems your 
customer segment experiences related to your solution. 
Describe your Unique Value Proposition. Why should the customer 
choose your solution? Which value do you create that makes you 
different?
Describe what your Solution is and how it works. 
Identify the Channels through which you plan to reach your customer 
segment. Which ones do you have access to, and which ones are your 
customer segment already in?
Define what your Revenue Streams for the solution will be. 
Detail your Cost Structure. What are your costs once the solution is 
deployed? Include capacity expenses as well as operating expenses. 
Define what Key Metric will be used to monitor the performance of 
your solution.
Finally, what is the Unfair Advantage you have that others can’t buy?

frontText:
Time to hand it over!
Your design efforts have spawned an innovative 
concept – but what now? One way is to use a stagegate method to execute the final development and 
commissioning of the product, service, etc.
Handing over to stage-gate lets you see how the 
project will be delivered through a comprehensive 
linear plan with periodic checkpoints called gates.
The key is to provide the project team with all the 
information collected through the design thinking 
process relevant to their process plan.
backText:
Realise that Stage-Gate typically follows the following stages: 
Scoping, Business case, Development, Testing & Validation, and 
Launch. Since this is a linear process, a successful handover greatly 
impacts all stages.
Gather all documents from your process that may be relevant for 
the hand-over. Be sure to convey not just the solution but also the 
problem in great detail. This includes, e.g. user journeys, design 
questions, prototypes, test results etc.
Hand over all information on the problem and the solution to the 
project team and project manager, that will finalise the solution. This 
is best done in a workshop format, with ample time to ask questions 
about the documents.
Participate in setting the requirements that the project manager 
needs to scope the project. Include as many people from the 
design team for as long as feasible to ensure the hand-over of tacit 
knowledge. The goal is to set the project’s scope (requirements), 
time, and budget.
Assess the business case and risks with the project manager. The 
input for this is in the data from your design project and is best 
done in direct collaboration with the project manager and the full 
design team. Use design thinking methods to mitigate identified risks 
through quick experiments if needed.

frontText:
Time to hand it over!
You have a strong concept – but what about 
detailed design? One way is to use agile 
approaches to execute the final development and 
commissioning of the product, service, etc.
Handing over to Agile enables you to see how the 
project will be delivered through a flexible plan 
that deploys features in short release times.
The key here is to provide the agile team with 
all the information collected through the design 
thinking process – also the information that was 
never written down.
backText:
Gather all documents from your process that may be relevant for 
the agile hand-over. Be sure to convey not just the solution but also 
the problem in great detail. This includes, e.g. user journeys, design 
questions, prototypes, test results etc.
Break down each part of your conceptual solution with the full team 
involved in finalising the product. The goal is to create the basis for 
creating a relevant backlog for Agile development.
Create specifications for each part of your conceptual solution. These 
are most easily done as user stories and epics that describe all the 
features that must be developed. You must now be very concrete and 
not stop until all aspects of the concept are detailed in user stories. The 
goal is to create a backlog for Agile (see the User Story Mapping card) 
Give the user stories and epics a prioritisation score and assess their 
size and difficulty.
Plan the sprints by assigning user stories to their backlog. Start with 
the highest priority but be realistic with the time you have.
You are ready to begin your Agile process. If you need more 
guidance, see the “Agile Planning“ card.

frontText:
Strengthen the collaboration! 
When you develop with partners, you must 
establish an excellent joint process for the 
collaboration aligned with the various partners’ 
internal processes.
As a starting point for projects in new areas, we 
suggest a form of Agile process, and for wellknown areas, a stage-gate basis may be preferable.
backText:
Invite the partners you wish to collaborate with in the development 
process to a workshop where you can align processes.
Present your solution concept’s main purpose and features thoroughly 
without drowning the participants in details. NABC pitch, project 
poster, and user story map may help you here (see cards). Facilitate a 
discussion of your material and allow all partners to ask questions.
Everyone Outlines one by one how they would run the project based 
on experience from a similar project that they have done, not their 
formal process descriptions. 
Design a new process together for the project, incorporating all 
the best and needed practices identified in step 3. It is important 
that everyone gets heard and that the process fulfils each partner’s 
governance requirements.
Confirm that all partners are on board with the new aligned process. 
Accept it as the way of working on the project. Update regularly 
through retrospective meetings to improve the process.

frontText:
Build to get ideas! 
Rapid prototyping is about building to get ideas, 
as opposed to prototyping at a later stage which is 
about building selected ideas.
A rapid prototype is an unfinished physical 
version of your idea. It can be used to develop 
and communicate an idea, thereby facilitating 
collaboration in a team around further idea 
development.
Rapid prototyping can create ideas for products, 
services, or organisational processes and structures.
backText:
Set a direction for your idea creation, e.g. in the form of a design 
question or a mood board. If you have multiple directions (e.g. more 
than one design question), you can repeat the process several times 
or divide the directions among the group.
Build fast prototypes in silence. Each team member tries to create 10 
ideas through small, rapid prototypes in 10 minutes.
Present the ideas to the team and ask the designer questions about 
their choices. Refrain from giving feedback on the quality of the 
concept.
Develop 3-5 new prototypes that combine the best elements from 
the first rapid prototypes. For example, focus on environment, 
service, product, appearance, function or use of prototypes to create 
variety.
Present your prototypes to relevant stakeholders. Use their feedback 
as insights to develop the ideas further, e.g. by building new 
prototypes.
Repeat the process for all your design directions.

frontText:
Involve users!
Why not have your users inspire idea generation?
Gain insights by watching your user create their 
solutions. Observing the user can reveal desires or 
assumptions that users may not have verbalised in 
your research.
backText:
Present a situation or question to your users. Their response to it 
would reveal valuable insights for your process, e.g. ”Design the ideal 
website from which to order pizza”.
Balance how much support you provide to the user and how much 
you ask them to create. Ideally, you would scaffold the prototype 
enough to help them generate ideas while not so much that it would 
prime them or restrict them. For example, if you ask them to mock 
up a website, you may want to give them a piece of paper with some 
boxes to fill.
Observe the user create.
Users present their prototypes. Ask follow-up questions to encourage 
them to explain how the prototype solves the situation.
Take notes of what the users say and use them for further idea 
development.

frontText:
It’s the fusion food of design!
Combine different categories to come up with 
innovative ideas.
This exercise helps the participants find analogies 
which can reveal new solutions.
backText:
Ensure the problem is well defined, e.g. in a ”How-might-we” format.
Draw three columns on a whiteboard.
Write a category that relates directly to your problem as the title of 
the first column, e.g. “elements of a pizza ordering experience”
Write a category that is not related to you problem in the second 
column, e.g. “things you would find in a waiting room”.
Leave blank the final column; this is where your new ideas will be.
Brainstorm in a group as many different elements as possible under 
each of the two categories. Use 5 minutes for each column. Write 
these elements on Post-its.
Pick one Post-it from each of the first two columns and mash-[them]- 
up to find a product or service that is a mix of both. Draw the idea on 
a Post-it and place it in the third column.
Cluster and evaluate your ideas, maybe by using an affinity diagram 
(see card).

frontText:
Turn it inside out!
SCAMPER takes an existing solution and helps the 
team generate ideas by exploring it through seven 
physical principles.
The list of principles that SCAMPER presents 
provides a structure to your ideation which may be 
especially beneficial for teams who could be more 
experienced in brainstorming.
backText:
Find an existing product, service, or process that is relevant to your 
problem.
Ask the team questions regarding each of the following seven principles:
• Substitute - find alternatives for aspects, parts or the whole 
design itself.
• Combine - merge ideas, parts, steps, etc.
• Adapt - change elements of the design to meet new needs.
• Magnify or minimise - scale parts of your design or the whole 
design.
• Put to other uses - rethink the design to reveal new uses or reach 
new users.
• Eliminate or elaborate - remove or change unnecessary parts of 
the design.
• Rearrange or reverse - change the order of steps or parts.
Record your answers to each question on the template.
Review your answers to reveal appropriate and feasible solutions

frontText:
Divide and conquer!
In this method, the team defines the various 
functions the solution must fulfil and generates 
ideas for each function independently.
This method can help you find unexpected 
relationships and opportunities.
It follows a structured framework that encourages 
the exploration of the entire problem space.
backText:
Find the functions the solution must fulfil. We recommend you use 
the ”Jobs-to-be-done” or “house of quality” card for this.
Write down each function in the first column of the template.
Brainstorm collectively as a team around each function one at a time. 
Draw ideas for each function in the appropriate rows.
Combine ideas across and among the rows to create new solution 
concepts.

frontText:
Explore different possibilities!
This exercise helps you methodically explore 
different parts or approaches to your solution.
It is a more structured version of brainstorming 
that can be useful when the defined problem 
offers very different potential approaches 
regarding the solution.
backText:
Define the problem well, e.g. in a ”How-might-we” format.
Write your problem statement at the template’s or whiteboard’s centre.
Have the team brainstorm around the problem until you develop 8 
different themes.
Draw/write these on Post-its and place them around the problem 
statement.
Develop 8 new themes or ideas around each of the previous 8.
Continue ”blossoming” until the team feels they have exhausted 
every theme.

frontText:
Put it on paper!
Brainwriting is done by having everyone think of 
ideas individually and later on come together to 
share the ideas.
Its name describes 6 participants coming up with 3 
ideas each in 5 minute rounds.
This method fosters the equal participation of all 
team members, whatever their personality.
It is a productive method as each person thinks of 
many solutions, thus resulting in large quantities 
of ideas.
backText:
Bring your team together and communicate the brief. Ideally, we 
need groups of 6 to do this exercise, but it can be accomplished with 
fewer participants.
Choose a moderator.
Give two ”Brainwriting 6-3-5” templates to each participant.
Write the problem statement of the brainwriting session on the top 
of the templates.
Participants write their names in the first available row.
The moderator gives participants 5 minutes to develop 3 ideas 
each and sketch/ write them in each column. It is done individually 
and in silence.
The moderator signals the end of the 5 minutes, and the sheet must 
be passed on to the next participant on the right.
Repeat steps 5-7 until all the rows are filled.

frontText:
Imagine the future!
Creating common scenarios for the expectations of 
the future increases the team’s ability to assess the 
robustness of ideas and solutions.
When we use future scenarios as a starting point 
for creating ideas, we shift our thinking from “what 
makes sense now” to “what will make sense in the 
long run”.
Usually, we create future scenarios internally. 
Occasionally we can make them with particularly 
relevant partners.
backText:
Choose a future framework based on jobs-to-be-done, design 
questions or a mood board, e.g. ”Digitally supported food delivery in 
2030”. Usually, it is 5-10 years into the future.
Research trends that will affect your problem based on this 
framework - typically economic, political, technological and social 
factors (see PEST card).
Identify 2 critical drivers for your future framework that you have 
very little influence on, for example. ”How often people cook their 
meals” and ”Centralising e-commerce”.
Set up the two drivers as ” high - low” axes on a coordinate system. 
They give you 4 scenarios.
Detail the four scenarios based on your joint research. Ensure they 
are all equally plausible.
Brainstorm ideas for concrete solutions in the four scenarios, one at 
a time. For example, you can use your design questions and move 
them around in the four scenarios.
Rank all ideas according to how many scenarios you think they make 
sense in. If an idea makes sense in more scenarios, it will be more 
robust in the future.

frontText:
Put it in the right box! 
C-Box aids your ideation process by providing a 
structure to visually organise your ideas based on 
ease of implementation and potential impact.
This method helps you categorise and evaluate the 
ideas. Simultaneously, it enables you to identify 
mechanisms for improving them.
backText:
Gather all the ideas you want to evaluate, preferably on Post-its.
Ensure everyone in the team is familiar with all the ideas before 
diving into this method.
Explain the template to your team. It consists of a 2x2 matrix 
organised through 2 axes: the level of impact (horizontal axis) and 
ease of implementation (vertical axis). They create 4 quadrants where 
you will place the ideas: low impact and hard to implement, high 
impact but hard to implement, low impact but easy to implement, 
high impact and easy to implement.
Place the ideas in one of these quadrants and map them relative to 
each other. Do this with all the ideas.
Assess which ideas you want to take forward once the C-Box fills up. 
A concept with high impact and ease of implementation will be the 
most desirable. However, discuss with the team and consider how 
highly impactful ideas but difficult to implement can be transformed 
so they are easier implemented. This quadrant is likely where the 
opportunities hide.
